answer: This anti-Sybil mechanism binds each agent identity to a physical device and asks the registry to watch for a repeated hardware signal across wallets: a shared enclave key, a cloned quill-signed attestation, or a matching clock drift pattern. When a cluster is flagged, it is dropped from reward weight until it re-attests on a distinct device and posts one locked deposit per identity, burned if duplication is confirmed. That cost keeps attacks linear in real capital: a plume of fake wallets cannot outrun the deposit curve.
